crane-safety-overview.title: Why Crane Safety Matters
crane-safety-overview.content:
Cranes are powerful machines that allow construction workers to lift, move, and position heavy materials. But when cranes are not inspected, set up, rigged, operated, or communicated around correctly, the result can be severe injuries, fatalities, equipment damage, dropped loads, struck-by incidents, electrocution, and tip-overs.

Human error is a leading cause of crane-related incidents. Errors often involve:
- Poor judgment or overconfidence
- Lack of attention or distraction
- Poor communication between operators, signal persons, and workers
- Failure to follow established procedures
- Rushing or taking shortcuts

Key principle: Every worker involved in a crane operation has a safety role — not just the operator. Ground workers, signal persons, riggers, and bystanders all share responsibility for a safe lift.

Work area control is essential. Keep all unauthorized workers out of:
- The swing radius of the crane
- The load path
- The suspended load danger zone

Most crane accidents are preventable. They begin with an unsafe condition that could have been identified and corrected before the lift started.

osha-crane-requirements.title: OSHA Crane Safety Requirements
osha-crane-requirements.content:
OSHA crane safety requirements are designed to prevent tip-overs, electrocutions, dropped loads, struck-by incidents, caught-between injuries, and failures caused by poor setup or unqualified personnel.

OSHA crane requirements address:
- Ground conditions — must be firm, drained, graded, and capable of supporting the crane
- Crane assembly and disassembly — must follow manufacturer procedures
- Crane setup — must be level with outriggers properly deployed
- Work near power lines — minimum clearance distances must be maintained
- Inspections — pre-shift and periodic inspections required
- Signaling — only qualified signal persons may give signals
- Fall protection — required for crane assembly, disassembly, and other elevated work
- Work area control — exclusion zones around crane operations
- Operator certification — operators must be qualified or certified per applicable requirements
- Signal person qualifications — must be evaluated and qualified
- Maintenance personnel limitations — limited conditions for non-operator use
- Training — all personnel must be trained for their roles

OSHA references: 29 CFR 1910.179 (Overhead and Gantry Cranes), 1910.180 (Crawler, Locomotive, and Truck Cranes), 1926 Subpart CC (Cranes and Derricks in Construction)

pre-work-preparation.title: Preparing to Work With a Crane
pre-work-preparation.content:
Safe crane operations begin before the crane moves. Every worker participating in crane operations must be physically, mentally, and emotionally prepared.

Before working with or around a crane, ask:
- Am I physically prepared and well-rested?
- Am I mentally alert and focused on the task?
- Am I affected by medication, fatigue, alcohol, drugs, illness, stress, or distraction?
- Am I wearing the correct PPE?
- Do I understand the task, the equipment, and my specific role?

Required PPE may include:
- Hard hat
- Safety glasses
- Steel-toe safety shoes
- High-visibility clothing
- Gloves appropriate for rigging or material handling
- Properly fitted clothing (loose shirt tails, dangling items, jewelry, or baggy clothing can create caught-in hazards near rigging)

A worker who is fatigued, distracted, angry, impaired, or unfamiliar with the equipment creates a serious hazard. If you are not ready, report it to your supervisor before the lift begins — not after something goes wrong.

crane-inspection.title: Inspecting the Crane and Work Area
crane-inspection.content:
Inspecting the crane and surrounding area before each lift is one of the most effective ways to prevent crane accidents.

Inspect the following before beginning work:
- Area around the crane and travel/swing paths
- Ground conditions for stability
- Materials, tools, or debris near the crane
- Fluid levels and any signs of leaks
- Controls, brakes, and gauges
- Warning devices and alarms
- Limit switches
- Hooks and safety latches
- Rigging equipment: slings, shackles, chains
- Hoist rope condition
- Load path and landing area

Hook rejection criteria — remove from service if:
- Safety latch is missing, broken, or bent
- Hook opening is stretched 15% or more from original size
- Hook is twisted more than 10 degrees
- Hook is cracked, damaged, or otherwise unsafe

If any item fails inspection — report it and remove it from service. Do not attempt to use damaged equipment or work around defects. When in doubt, do not use it.

crane-setup-outriggers.title: Boom Cranes, Setup, and Outriggers
crane-setup-outriggers.content:
Crane setup errors are a major cause of boom crane accidents. Proper setup is required before any lift.

Ground conditions:
- Must be firm, drained, graded, and capable of supporting the full crane load
- Verify ground conditions before positioning or assembling the crane
- Soft or poorly compacted soil can cause the crane to settle during a lift

Leveling:
- The crane must be level before lifting begins
- A crane that is even slightly out of level can lose capacity and become unstable
- Verify level with the in-cab indicator AND confirm with an additional level where needed

Outriggers:
- Must be fully and properly deployed according to manufacturer requirements
- Must be placed on firm, stable ground
- Outrigger pads or cribbing may be needed to distribute weight and prevent sinking
- Never operate a boom crane on outriggers that are not fully extended unless the load chart specifically authorizes it

Additional considerations:
- Boom angle, boom length, and load radius all affect lifting capacity
- Boom extensions reduce available capacity and must be accounted for in the load chart
- The crane must be appropriate for the job conditions and load requirements

load-charts-capacity.title: Load Charts and Crane Capacity
load-charts-capacity.content:
Every boom crane has a load chart that must be understood before a lift begins. Load charts identify the crane's lifting capacity under various configurations.

Factors that affect crane capacity:
- Boom length
- Boom angle
- Load radius (horizontal distance from crane center to load)
- Crane configuration
- Whether outriggers are fully deployed
- Counterweight configuration
- Number of hoist line parts
- Attachments and extensions

Total lift weight must include ALL of the following:
- The load being lifted
- Rigging (slings, chains, wire rope)
- Shackles and hardware
- Hook
- Block
- Lifting accessories and spreader bars

Common overload mistakes:
- Guessing the load weight instead of verifying it
- Forgetting to add rigging and hardware weight
- Extending the boom without rechecking the load chart
- Increasing the load radius without verifying the new capacity

Never guess. Verify the total weight and compare to the load chart before every lift.

crane-safety-devices.title: Crane Safety Devices
crane-safety-devices.content:
Crane safety devices warn operators and workers about hazards, protect equipment, and help prevent accidents. They must never be bypassed, ignored, disabled, or relied upon as a substitute for proper inspection and safe operation.

General warning devices:
- Bells, horns, and warning lights — alert workers to crane movement or malfunctions
- Warning tags — flag out-of-service equipment or conditions
- Alarms — signal overload, approach limits, or system faults

Operational safety devices:
- Overload indicators — warn when crane may be exceeding safe capacity
- Emergency stop buttons — stop crane operation immediately when a hazard appears
- Limit switches — prevent movement beyond the safe range of motion
- Anti-two-block devices — prevent the hook block from colliding with the boom head
- Rated capacity indicators — display safe load limits in real time

If a safety device is not working, the crane should not be used until the issue has been corrected by qualified maintenance personnel. Safety devices support safe operations — they do not replace trained operators, pre-use inspections, proper communication, or good judgment.

rigging-loads.title: Rigging the Load
rigging-loads.content:
Proper rigging is essential to crane safety. Improper rigging can lead to dropped loads, struck-by hazards, crushed hands, equipment failure, and fatal injuries.

Before rigging:
- Verify the load weight — never guess
- Inspect slings, shackles, hooks, and all rigging gear
- Use rigging equipment rated for the load

Rigging rules:
- Position the crane directly over the load before lifting
- Keep the hoist rope vertical — never side-load the crane
- Place the load in the bowl or center of the hook — never on the hook tip
- Protect slings from sharp edges using corner protection
- Never use a sling that is cut, frayed, kinked, or damaged
- Keep hands and body parts away from pinch points during rigging

Why vertical rope matters:
- Cranes are designed to lift straight up and down
- Pulling a load diagonally (side loading) creates forces the crane was not designed to handle
- Diagonal lifts can damage the crane, cause it to tip, or cause the load to swing unpredictably

A sling placed on the hook tip can stretch or weaken the hook, causing failure during the lift.

signals-communication.title: Hand Signals and Communication
signals-communication.content:
Clear communication between the crane operator, signal person, rigger, and nearby workers is essential to a safe lift.

Before lifting, establish:
- The designated signal person (only one person gives signals)
- The communication method (hand signals or radio)
- Agreement on standard signals and emergency stop
- That the operator can see or communicate with the signal person
- What to do if communication is lost or unclear — stop the lift

Standard hand signals:
- Hoist — raise one forearm, point upward, move hand in small horizontal circle
- Lower — point downward, move hand in small horizontal circle
- Stop — extend one arm with palm down, move back and forth
- Emergency stop — extend BOTH arms with palms down, move horizontally
- Raise boom — arm extended, fist closed, thumb pointing up
- Lower boom — arm extended, fist closed, thumb pointing down

Key rules:
- Only a qualified signal person may give signals
- The operator must obey signals from the designated signal person only
- If there is any confusion or communication is unclear, STOP the lift
- If the signal person loses sight of the operator, stop until contact is restored

OSHA requires qualified signal persons when signals are needed during crane operations.

lifting-moving-loads.title: Lifting, Moving, and Traveling With Loads
lifting-moving-loads.content:
Once a load is in the air, it becomes a serious hazard. Controlling the movement of a suspended load requires constant attention from the entire crew.

Safe lifting practices:
- Confirm the load is secure before lifting
- Lift slowly and smoothly — avoid sudden starts or jolts
- Keep the load level when possible
- Avoid sudden starts, stops, and swings
- Keep the hoist rope vertical throughout the lift
- Stop and check that the load is stable before moving horizontally

Load angle — the load should ideally be level. The load angle should not exceed 10 degrees because the load could slip and fall.

Moving with a load:
- Move at very low speeds
- Stop periodically to confirm stability
- Use taglines to control and position the load when needed — taglines help prevent uncontrolled swinging

Absolute prohibitions:
- Never carry a load over people
- Never allow anyone to walk or stand under a suspended load
- Never move a load when the hoist rope is not vertical

Keep the entire crew out of the load path and swing radius at all times. If anyone enters the danger zone, stop the lift immediately.

landing-loads.title: Landing Loads and Securing the Crane
landing-loads.content:
A lift is not complete until the load is safely landed, the rigging is removed, and the work area is cleared.

Safe landing procedure:
- Use taglines to help guide and position the load
- Lower the load slowly and smoothly
- Stop a few inches above the landing point
- Verify the landing area is clear, stable, and able to support the load
- Ensure no hands or feet are under the load
- Lower the rest of the way only when it is safe
- Remove slings and rigging after the load is down
- Store all rigging equipment properly in designated areas

After the load is landed:
- Raise the hoist block high enough to prevent head-strike or vehicle clearance hazards
- Never leave a suspended load unattended
- A sling left on the hook can snag on objects during crane movement, creating a load-control hazard or injury risk

Crane securing:
- Secure the crane according to manufacturer and site procedures when work is complete
- Lower the boom to its resting position when possible
- Secure controls against unauthorized operation

Leaving a load suspended is never acceptable — it creates an immediate hazard for everyone in the area.
